thread.title: Multiple Positive Developments Are Not Yet Reflected In Super Micro's Shares - Super Micro Computer, Inc. (NASDAQ:SMCI)

author: CVC Research
title: Multiple Positive Developments Are Not Yet Reflected In Super Micro's Shares - Super Micro Computer, Inc. (NASDAQ:SMCI)
text:
I have written several bullish takes on Super Micro ( SMCI ) since August when their stock took a big hit on the notice that their stock would be delisted from Nasdaq due to a delay in getting their filings current (which is due to an ongoing accounting review).
Since that time, I have remained positive, despite a subsequent (and presumably unrelated) story published by Bloomberg in early October claiming that Chinese spies had managed to implant small "spy chips" on SMCI server motherboards manufactured in China. For those of you that have followed this story like I have, this is old news, but very quickly named SMCI customers like Apple ( AAPL ) and Amazon ( AMZN ) publicly stated the story was inaccurate.
The purpose of this article is to update on key developments since my last article and to give an updated view on the stock.
Q119 Results (Sept '18 quarter) and Update on Restatement In mid-November the company reported a great set of results along with filing an 8-K that showed the expected change in Revenue and EPS during the anticipated restatement period covering FY15-FY17.
First, the company reported Revenue/EPS of ~$957M/$0.68 versus consensus of $838M/$0.44. Note that these are still preliminary estimates, as the company still has an ongoing accounting review. Revenue growth accelerated to 41% Y/Y, the highest Y/Y quarterly revenue growth rate in over 3 years. Clearly, these were great numbers relative to expectations. One important thing to note also in these results was that they saw a 40 basis point sequential uptick in GMs from 12.9% to 13.3% in the quarter. This is an important point because recently, despite record revenues, SMCI GMs have been under pressure and below its own historical range due to high component (input) pricing, particularly memory. As memory prices have now started declining, SMCI is only beginning to see the GM benefit show up in their reported results. Historically GMs have been closer to ~15%, which is well above the most recent quarter's 13.3%. For a business operating at fairly slim ~5% operating margins, a normalization of GMs towards their historical norms would provide a significant EPS uplift, independent of any further revenue growth.
Source: Sentieo
The company provided only narrow ranges rather than precise numbers regarding its updated FY15-FY17 Revenue/EPS, but it was enough to see that the restatement is close to wrapping up, in my opinion, and that the changes to historical results will be fairly immaterial.
Source: Company filings, CVC analysis
Here is the full range of updated historical revised numbers provided in the SMCI 8-K :
This disclosure went a long way, in my mind, towards putting to rest the accounting overhang. We can see that the expected restatement of 3 years of financials results in an immaterial ~1% negative impact on revenue and ~3% negative impact on EPS cumulatively over the three year period (FY15-FY17), using the midpoints of the provided ranges. And, given the reasonably tight revised revenue and EPS ranges provided, even using the low end of each would still not result in what I would consider a material downward revision of those prior results.
Is Bloomberg Set to Retract "Big Hack" Story? In a separate positive development the Washington Post reported recently that Bloomberg has assigned a new reporter to re-investigate the controversial "China Hack" story, which implies doubts Bloomberg has about their reporting (not surprising given Tim Cook of AAPL had already publicly called for a retraction of the story, saying it was false). Here's an excerpt from the Washington Post article (emphasis mine):
Bloomberg has continued reporting the blockbuster story that it broke on Oct. 4, including a very recent round of inquiries from a Bloomberg News/Bloomberg Businessweek investigative reporter. In emails to employees at Apple, Bloomberg’s Ben Elgin has requested “discreet” input on the alleged hack. “My colleagues’ story from last month (Super Micro) has sparked a lot of pushback ,” Elgin wrote on Nov. 19 to one Apple employee. “I’ve been asked to join the research effort here to do more digging on this … and I would value hearing your thoughts (whatever they may be) and guidance, as I get my bearings.”
One person who spoke with Elgin told the Erik Wemple Blog that the Bloomberg reporter made clear that he wasn’t part of the reporting team that produced “The Big Hack.” The goal of this effort, Elgin told the potential source, was to get to “ground truth” ; if Elgin heard from 10 or so sources that “The Big Hack” was itself a piece of hackery, he would send that message up his chain of command. The potential source told Elgin that the denials of “The Big Hack” were “100 percent right.”
The key point here is that Bloomberg is re-investigating using a new reporter (Ben Elgin), not the original "China Hack" author (Jordan Robertson). We shall see what comes of the Bloomberg re-investigation, but I suspect it will end in a mea culpa, acknowledging that the original reporter either got his facts wrong, was misled, or some other excuse I haven't yet thought of. This would serve to remove the other of the two key overhangs currently depressing the stock (the other being the accounting review/restatement obviously).
Latest Update From SMCI On 12/11/18, SMCI just published an 8-K that disclosed two key items: 1) SMCI's third party investigation found no evidence to support the "China Hack" story's claims, 2) SMCI has sent a letter to its customers explaining the same. While one may be inclined to roll their eyes at the 'accused' claiming innocence, I actually find this quite meaningful. Should SMCI know about or have found evidence of the supposed "hack," it would not be in their interest, in my opinion, to claim otherwise in a letter to customers. This minimally exposes them to a serious loss in credibility/confidence amongst customers, and potentially some (or additional) legal liability. Simply put, I believe they did an investigation (they put that in an SEC filing) and they did not find anything indicating any hacking had occurred.
Stock Implications So now, let's come back to the stock. Based on the current share price of 16.50, SMCI still only trades at ~6x run-rate EPS and below my estimated TBV of ~$18. Please also see my earlier article on why I believe TBV is materially understated due to SMCI's large (and very valuable) real estate holdings; I believe "true" TBV is actually more like $25/share. As to the current ~6x EPS multiple, one can compare this to its historical near-market multiple (as measured relative to the S&P 500) and it's clear that this earnings multiple today remains far too low. The company's historical growth has justified this at/above market multiple and the most recent quarter's record results showing 40%+ Y/Y revenue growth certainly doesn't argue against a premium multiple to the market for SMCI.
Source: Sentieo
Given their growth rate, I think an at/above market multiple will again be justified once filings are current and the stink of the (IMO totally false) Bloomberg story wears off. So I have no problem applying a market 15x multiple to current run-rate earnings of ~$2.70 and arriving at a $40+ price target. Once the above-mentioned overhangs are resolved, I believe this is reasonable.
Looking at it from a totally different angle, if one were to just believe that the Bloomberg "China Hack" story becomes formally discredited (likely by Bloomberg itself), SMCI stock was trading at 21.40 immediately before the Oct 4 release of the Bloomberg story. From today's prices, merely regaining that price level would represent a not-too-shabby 30% return from today's price.
Risks They do not get current on their filings and/or the preliminary restated numbers just disclosed prove too optimistic. Bloomberg story turns out to be at least somewhat accurate, causing huge damage to the reputation/brand, and results. Server/datacenter sales weaken substantially I don't have a strong point of view here. Obviously suppliers such as Intel ( INTC ) can be tracked. Also, datacenter CapEx plans from Alphabet ( GOOG ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), Amazon ( AMZN ), Facebook ( FB ), etc can be monitored. I would note again that even if sales growth for SMCI should turn negative (which hasn't happened - they guided to positive Y/Y revenue growth for the December quarter), they should have some nice headroom for GM expansion back to historical levels. Thus, they could theoretically show growing EPS even during a potential moderately declining revenue period. Disclosure: I am/we are long SMCI.
